corpus_definition: To stay in a place until something happens.

forms.note: No noun is made from await. Use the noun 'wait': 'a long wait for the results'.

forms.definition: to wait for something that is going to happen
forms.example: We are awaiting the results of the exam.
forms.note: No preposition after it: await the answer, not 'await for' the answer.

syn.note: The everyday way to say it; await is more formal.
Related: you think something will happen, but you are not always waiting for it.
Formal: you expect something and often prepare for it.
Related: you wait for something nice and feel happy about it.

forms.note: No adjective. The compound 'long-awaited' (a long-awaited film) is common but is a compound.

context.text: Students all over Uzbekistan are awaiting their exam results this week. Aziz is also awaiting a phone call from the university in Tashkent.

reviewer_note: Formal transitive verb; 'a-' is not a table affix, so no affix is claimed.

corpus_definition: Knowing about something that is happening or exists.
usage_note: be aware of + noun / -ing: 'Are you aware of the problem?' Also: be aware that + clause; well aware of / fully aware of for emphasis. Usually after a verb, not before a noun.

relations.note: Very close; conscious of is often about noticing something with your senses or feelings.
You know something well because you have seen or used it before.
You have been given information about something: 'well informed'.
Not knowing about something: 'He was unaware of the danger.'

context.text: Are you aware of the new bus timetable? Many people in our street were not aware of the change and missed the morning bus.

reviewer_note: Adjective + preposition phrase; noun awareness is not listed because phrases have no forms.

corpus_definition: For a short period of time.

forms.definition: a period of time, usually not very long
forms.example: I waited for a while, but nobody came.
forms.note: Awhile is made from 'a' + this noun. After 'for', write two words: for a while.

syn.note: Easy, general word: 'for some time'.
A moment is a very short time.
More formal: 'a period of two weeks'.

forms.note: No verb in this meaning. The phrasal verb 'while away' (spend time in a relaxed way) is separate.

forms.definition: for a short time
forms.example: Sit down and rest awhile before we go.
forms.note: Used straight after a verb: stay awhile, rest awhile. Many teachers say 'for awhile' is wrong; write 'for a while'.

syn.note: For a short time; also used for talking about something quickly.
For a limited time, not forever; more formal.
Easy and informal: 'Wait here for a bit.'

ant.note: For all time, with no end.
In a way that lasts for a very long time or always.

context.text: We were tired after the long walk, so we sat by the river and rested awhile. After a while, Dilnoza said it was time to go home.

reviewer_note: CORPUS: the example 'for awhile' is nonstandard in careful writing (prefer 'for a while'); map follows the definition and shows the correct use.

corpus_definition: An extra copy of information kept in case of loss.

forms.definition: an extra copy of computer files kept in case the first is lost
forms.example: Always keep a backup of your important files on another drive.
forms.note: Also written back-up in British English.

syn.note: Easy, general word; a backup is a copy kept for safety.
An exact copy; a little more formal.
An extra thing you keep in case you need it, like a spare key or tyre.

ant.note: The first, real version that copies are made from.

forms.definition: to make an extra copy of computer information
forms.example: I back up my photos every Sunday evening.
forms.note: As a verb it is written as two words: back up your files / back your files up.

syn.note: General word; back up means copying so you do not lose the files.
Related: to keep work on a computer; saving once is not the same as keeping a second copy.

forms.note: No adjective. Use the noun before another noun: a backup plan, a backup copy.

context.text: My laptop broke last month, but I didn't lose anything because I had a backup on a USB drive. Now I back up my files every week.

reviewer_note: Noun is one word (backup), verb is two (back up); this is the computer-copy sense, not support or a traffic jam.

forms.definition: a habit of becoming angry very quickly
forms.example: My older brother has a terrible temper.
forms.note: Common phrases: lose your temper, have a bad temper.

syn.note: Anger is the feeling; this word is about how quickly a person gets angry.
Formal: the state of getting annoyed easily.

ant.note: Staying calm when things are slow or difficult.

forms.definition: to make something less strong or extreme
forms.example: She tempered her criticism with a few kind words.
forms.note: Belongs to temper = soften or control, not getting angry. Formal.

forms.definition: often angry or annoyed, especially for small reasons
forms.example: The bad-tempered man shouted at the bus driver.

syn.note: Informal and easy; often about someone in a bad mood for a short time.
Gets annoyed easily, often because of being tired or ill.
British, a little informal: angry at one moment, not always.
Your mood changes quickly, often to unhappy or angry.

ant.note: Able to wait or deal with problems without getting angry.

forms.definition: in an angry, annoyed way
forms.example: He answered bad-temperedly and closed the door.

syn.note: Easy, general word.
British, a little informal.
Informal; in a bad mood.

ant.note: In a relaxed way, without anger.

context.text: Our neighbour is very bad-tempered in the mornings. Yesterday he lost his temper when the children played outside, and he spoke bad-temperedly to everyone.

reviewer_note: Compound adjective; the noun temper is the base it is made from. Good-tempered/ill-tempered left out of syn/ant because they share the family part.

corpus_definition: Food used to catch fish or other animals.

forms.definition: food put on a hook or in a trap to catch fish or animals
forms.example: He put some bait on the hook to catch fish.
forms.note: Uncountable: some bait, not a bait. Also used for anything that attracts people into a trap.

syn.note: Often a fake fish or object that attracts fish; also used for people.
Something used to trick an animal or person into coming closer.
A common kind of fishing food.

forms.definition: to put food on a hook or in a trap to catch animals
forms.example: My grandfather baited the hook with a piece of bread.
forms.note: Also means to annoy someone on purpose to make them angry (informal).

syn.note: To attract an animal or person, often with food or a trick.

context.text: Every Sunday my uncle goes fishing at Charvak Lake. He baits his hook with bread, because he says it is the best bait for carp.

reviewer_note: Verb bait also means to tease someone on purpose; mentioned in the verb note, map keeps the fishing sense.

corpus_definition: Having no hair on the top of your head.

forms.definition: the state of having little or no hair on your head
forms.example: Baldness often runs in families.

syn.note: Easy, common phrase; often used by doctors and in adverts.

forms.note: No verb. Say 'go bald' or 'lose your hair'.

forms.definition: with no hair, or very little hair, on the head
forms.example: My grandfather is completely bald.

syn.note: With no hair anywhere; less common for people's heads.
The hair has been cut off with a razor, on purpose.

forms.definition: starting to lose the hair on your head
forms.example: He was a short, balding man in a grey suit.

forms.definition: in a very direct way, without trying to be polite
forms.example: She told him baldly that his plan would not work.
forms.note: Belongs to bald = plain and direct (a bald statement), not about hair.

context.text: My father was already balding at thirty. Now he is completely bald, but he jokes that baldness saves him money at the barber's.

reviewer_note: False friend baldly (= bluntly) kept as other_meaning; no verb exists.

corpus_definition: A good price for something bought.

forms.definition: something you buy for less money than usual
forms.example: That jacket was a real bargain.

syn.note: Easy and very common: 'I got a good deal on this phone.'
Informal: something so cheap it is almost free.
Related: an agreement or offer; it needs 'good' to mean cheap.

ant.note: Informal: something that costs much too much.

forms.definition: to discuss a price with a seller to make it lower
forms.example: At Chorsu Bazaar, people often bargain with the sellers.
forms.note: Belongs to bargain = an agreement about a price, not a cheap thing you buy.
No adjective. Use the noun before another noun: bargain prices.

context.text: This bag was a real bargain: only fifty thousand sum at the market. My sister found another bargain at the same shop.

reviewer_note: Sense split: noun = cheap thing (this map); verb bargain = negotiate (agreement sense), shown as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: A round container made of wood or metal for storing liquids.

forms.definition: a large round container of wood or metal for liquids
forms.example: The old barrel was filled with fresh water.
forms.note: Also a unit for measuring oil: 'the price of oil per barrel'.

syn.note: A wooden one, usually for wine or beer.
A small metal one, usually for beer.
A large metal container for oil or chemicals.
Easy general word for anything that holds things.

forms.definition: to move very fast in a way that is hard to control
forms.example: The truck came barrelling down the hill.
forms.note: Belongs to barrel = move fast (informal), not the container. American spelling: barreling.

context.text: In my grandmother's garden there is a big metal barrel. She collects rain water in the barrel and uses it for her tomatoes.

reviewer_note: Informal verb barrel (move fast) kept as other_meaning.

corpus_definition: Part of the sea that goes into the land.

forms.definition: a part of the sea where the coast curves inwards
forms.example: We watched the boats in the bay.
forms.note: Often in names: the Bay of Bengal, San Francisco Bay.

syn.note: Usually much bigger: the Persian Gulf.
A small one, often with a beach.
A narrow part of the sea or a lake that goes into the land.
A safe place for boats near the coast. American spelling: harbor.

forms.definition: (of dogs or wolves) to make a long, deep, loud sound
forms.example: The dogs bayed at the moon all night.
forms.note: A different word with the same spelling, about dogs, not the sea.

context.text: Our hotel in Turkey looked over a quiet bay. Every morning, fishing boats left the bay and came back with fresh fish.

reviewer_note: Homonyms: bay (howl) is a separate word, shown as other_meaning with a note; bay window/parking bay left out.
